general.temas: Judicial decisions and political matters linked to the Supreme Court feature repeatedly, as do economic stories about companies and investments. Sports, health, leisure and consumer content also appear. Only Folha de S.Paulo highlights the damage caused by the rains in Paraná.
general.motivo_crispacion: Tensions are concentrated in stories about the Supreme Court, with Gazeta do Povo criticizing its justices and a councilwoman saying she was joking when she spoke about shooting Moraes. There are also disagreements between the government and mayors over funding for free transport, as well as pressure over a judicial appointment. Internationally, the conflict in Gaza and Russian threats highlighted by Poland stand out. Sports, consumer news and recipes partly offset this atmosphere.

Folha de S.Paulo.resumen:
- A federal court rejects a request to suspend the first battery auction for Brazil’s electricity sector.
- Narcisa Tamborindeguy recounts how she lost a lottery prize that was claimed by an employee.
- Luiz Carlos Trabuco replaces Jorge Gerdau as head of the board of the Competitive Brazil Movement.
- Rains cause damage in at least 50 cities in Paraná; arrests in Rio on suspicion of international human trafficking are also reported.
- The front page covers investments, corporate changes and mayors’ rejection of the proposed funding for free weekend transport.
Folha de S.Paulo.motivo_populismo: The language is predominantly factual, although the quote “The water just kept rising” adds drama and some headlines highlight multimillion-dollar losses or striking crimes, without invoking a confrontation between the people and the elites.
Folha de S.Paulo.sesgo: The selection gives particular weight to the economy, investments and corporate developments, alongside crime and entertainment news. There is no clear partisan bias in the headlines provided.

O Globo.resumen:
- The new generation of the Batista family prepares to take over at JBS.
- A symposium on Black Consciousness brings together judicial representatives, artists and athletes in São Paulo.
- Rising computer prices are driving the refurbishment of used components; another story covers the use of AI to find coupons.
- In sports, highlights include Thiago Silva’s contract renewal, Flamengo’s search for a coach and the meeting between Neymar and Neto.
- The Senate approves a bill on the SUS National Force; a Salvadoran mistakenly deported from the U.S. arrives in Spain.
O Globo.motivo_populismo: The tone is predominantly factual, although expressions such as “legal battle,” “controversies” and “emotion” add drama; there is no apparent appeal to the people against the elites.
O Globo.sesgo: The selection devotes considerable space to sports and combines business, consumer and service news with institutional affairs. Some sports headlines emphasize emotion and controversy, but there is no clear political bias.

O Estado de S. Paulo.resumen:
- A reader’s question asks how to address the violence in GTA 6 with teenagers.
- Black Eyed Peas will perform in São Paulo for people who complete four hours of volunteer work.
- An analysis identifies nine profitable, publicly traded companies with low debt.
- Alcolumbre pressures Lula to accept Pacheco for the STF; the TCU withdraws fines against members of Dilma Rousseff’s government.
- The front page also covers the cancer vaccine, the Libertadores final, the genocide trial in Myanmar and consumer, film and cooking content.
O Estado de S. Paulo.motivo_populismo: The tone is predominantly factual and service-oriented, although expressions such as “fascinating” and “the most technologically advanced in history” add promotional emphasis.
O Estado de S. Paulo.sesgo: The selection combines politics and justice with entertainment, consumer news and practical advice, with a notable focus on serving readers. There is no clear political bias across the headlines.

Gazeta do Povo.resumen:
- Israel killed Hamas’s internal security chief in northern Gaza, following another operation against a commander of the group.
- Two articles question judicial decisions concerning Marcel van Hattem and Jair Bolsonaro; another reports that Moraes rejected a budget request.
- Several stories cover the Catholic Church, Pope Francis’s spiritual life and an initiative to invite people to Mass.
- A Christian woman will stand trial in England for praying silently near an abortion clinic.
- The front page also carries news about Argentina, Poland’s air defense and the Miss Universe winner.
Gazeta do Povo.motivo_populismo: The comparison of the Supreme Court to AI-5, the question “Who is afraid of Jair Bolsonaro?” and the expression “perk” introduce confrontation and emotional weight, although many headlines are factual.
Gazeta do Povo.sesgo: The selection pays particular attention to Catholic topics and takes a critical view of Supreme Court decisions, associating them with censorship and dictatorship. The rest of the front page includes international and social affairs, generally in more descriptive language.

CartaCapital.resumen:
- The STF examines budget amendments, the carrying of firearms by municipal guards and research involving human subjects; Moraes closed another investigation into posts linking Bolsonaro to cannibalism.
- A councilwoman says her comment about shooting Moraes was a joke; in Mato Grosso, police are investigating an officer’s assault on an autistic child.
- A study forecasts an economic impact of 8.8 billion reais from the Women’s World Cup; another story questions Banco de Brasil loans ahead of a change in its leadership.
- The Army detonated toxic explosives in Iowa despite fears of contamination.
- The front page also offers cassava and moqueca recipes and a Chinese horoscope for December.
CartaCapital.motivo_populismo: The tone is predominantly factual, although expressions such as “in the crosshairs,” “despite fears” and “has other things to answer for” add drama or critical judgment.
CartaCapital.sesgo: The selection gives prominence to the STF and to security and public administration issues. The Banco de Brasil story takes a critical approach to its loans and the selection of its next leadership.

opiniones.comunista:
I see in today’s news a dispute over who pays and who decides. Mayors reject funding free weekend fares with parliamentary budget amendments because they consider them unstable. I share that concern: transport is a right; it cannot depend on funding allocations subject to political negotiation. We need permanent public funding and control by workers and users.

The court’s refusal to suspend the battery auction also raises a question: will strategic infrastructure serve private profit or collective needs? I advocate public ownership and democratic control of the electricity system. The rains that have caused damage in dozens of cities in Paraná are also a reminder of why we need public services capable of responding to emergencies. The Senate’s approval of the bill to consolidate the SUS National Force points in that direction.
opiniones.anarquista:
The rains have caused damage in at least 50 cities in Paraná. Faced with an emergency like this, I think of the power of mutual aid: neighbors able to organize freely to share shelter, food and care. Not as an excuse for institutions to abandon their responsibilities, but as a way for communities to decide and act without waiting for orders from above.

I am also concerned that free weekend fares depend on funding that mayors consider unstable. Getting around should not be a privilege or a promise subject to disputes between parties. I want accessible transport, managed with genuine participation from workers and users.

And the allegation of a police assault on an autistic child at a school in Mato Grosso is a reminder of why I distrust all armed authority: care requires listening and autonomy, not obedience.
opiniones.liberal:
The proposal for free transport on weekends deserves a simple question: who pays, and how secure is the funding? Mayors reject funding it with parliamentary budget amendments because they consider them unstable. I share the concern: a zero fare does not eliminate the cost; it merely shifts it. I prefer targeted, transparent assistance to universal promises backed by uncertain resources.

I also welcome the fact that the debate over electricity-sector batteries continues after the court’s decision not to suspend the auction. But an auction does not in itself guarantee competition: I demand clear rules, open access and attention to the cost to consumers, without privileges for companies chosen by those in power.

My ideal is a limited state that protects rights and is accountable, lower taxes, and citizens free to make decisions and take responsibility. Prosperity is better fostered by competition than by political discretion.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
I worry that Brazil is confusing governing with handing out promises. Mayors reject funding free weekend transport with parliamentary budget amendments because they consider that source unstable. They are right to demand accountability: a policy that brings benefits today but has no secure funding tomorrow ends up weakening municipalities and punishing taxpayers.

I also see a question of sovereignty in the battery auction for the electricity sector, which will go ahead following the court decision. It is not enough to celebrate investment: I want to know what guarantees there will be for energy security and the national interest. Business and political elites should not decide strategic matters as though citizens were spectators.

And in the face of the rains that have caused damage in dozens of cities in Paraná, the priority must be to protect families and help rebuild their communities. That too is defending the nation.
opiniones.centro:
I see the same demand running through today’s news: turning good intentions into lasting policies. Free weekend transport fares can expand opportunities, but mayors are right to ask for stable funding. I would prefer an agreement between municipalities and the government that identifies sustainable resources to a promise of a benefit whose continuation remains in doubt.

I also welcome the Senate’s approval of a bill to give the SUS National Force legal stability. The rains that have caused damage in dozens of cities in Paraná are a reminder of the value of having public services prepared for emergencies. For me, protecting the population and keeping the public finances in order are not opposing goals: both require capable institutions, coordination and reforms that can be sustained beyond a single term in office.
